Now, imagine you have a fast, slightly sloppy intern who can scribble down a draft in seconds. Speculative decoding works by leveraging this dynamic between two models: a large, slow "target" model and a smaller, fast "draft" model.

In standard text generation, the large model generates one token at a time, waiting for each calculation to finish before starting the next. This is sequential and slow. Speculative decoding changes the workflow. First, the small draft model quickly generates a sequence of candidate tokens, say five words, in a single pass. Because it is small, it is fast, but it might be less accurate.

Next, these candidate tokens are fed into the large target model. Crucially, the large model processes all these candidates in parallel, not sequentially. It evaluates the probability of each token given the previous context. If the large model agrees with the draft’s choices, it accepts them. If it disagrees, it rejects the draft’s token and generates its own correct token for that position. The process then continues from that point.

The key insight is that the large model’s final output is mathematically identical to what it would have produced if it had generated the text token-by-token on its own. The draft model does not influence the final content; it only provides a guess to speed up the verification process. If the draft is good, the large model accepts multiple tokens at once, effectively skipping several slow sequential steps. If the draft is bad, the large model corrects it, but the penalty is minimal because the large model was going to generate that correct token anyway.

This technique is safe because the acceptance criteria are based on the target model’s own probability distribution. It ensures that the statistical properties of the generated text remain unchanged. You are not changing the model’s mind; you are just asking it to verify a batch of guesses faster than it would have written them from scratch. For a new engineer, think of it as a "look-ahead" optimization. It trades a small amount of compute for the small model against a significant reduction in latency for the large model, resulting in faster generation without sacrificing quality or altering the underlying logic of the text.

A hash map starts life as a fixed array of slots, each slot holding either nothing or a reference to a chain of entries. When you ask the map to store a key-value pair, it runs the key through a hash function, which spits out an integer. That integer gets wrapped around by taking a remainder (mod) against the array's length, giving you an index into the array. In the best case, that slot is empty and you just plop the entry in and walk away.

The trouble starts when two different keys hash to the same slot. This is a collision, and it's guaranteed to happen eventually once your collection grows past a certain size, because the hash function can only produce a finite number of distinct outputs. The most common way to deal with it is called chaining: the slot doesn't just hold one entry, it holds a small linked list (or vector) of all the entries that happened to hash there. When a new key lands in an already-occupied slot, you compare it against the entries in the chain one by one. If you find a match, you update its value. If not, you append the new entry to the end of that chain. Lookups and deletions work the same way — hash to the slot, then walk the chain until you find the right key. The cost of this chain walk is what keeps the hash map from being a pure O(1) operation, but as long as the chains stay short, the average cost remains close to constant.

A less common but still widely used alternative is open addressing, where the map refuses to let a slot hold a chain. Instead, when the target slot is taken, it probes to the next slot, then the next, and so on, using a deterministic pattern (linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing) to decide where to look next. The entry gets stored in the first empty slot it finds. This can be faster for cache locality since everything lives in one contiguous array, but it requires a sentinel value to mark "deleted" slots and can degrade badly if the table fills up.

Either way, the underlying principle is the same: as you keep inserting entries, the average chain length (or probe length) creeps upward, and each operation starts to cost more. The map tracks a ratio called the load factor — roughly, the number of occupied slots divided by the total number of slots. When that ratio crosses a threshold (typically somewhere around 0.75, though it varies by implementation), the map decides it's time to resize.

Resizing means allocating a brand-new, larger array — usually double the old one — and then rehashing every single entry into it. Each key gets its hash recomputed (or at least its index recomputed with the new modulo), and it gets placed into its new slot in the bigger array. Because the array is now twice as large, the average chain length drops back down, and the map regains its fast average-case performance. The one-time cost of rehashing everything sounds expensive, but because you do it rarely relative to the number of operations you actually perform, the *amortized* cost of an insert remains constant. In practice, a sequence of, say, 1,000 inserts might trigger one resize at entry 768 (if the threshold is 0.75 on a 1,024-slot table), and the map will quietly double its size, rehash all 768 entries into a 2,044-slot array, and then continue on as if nothing happened.

The core problem it solves is that these models are inherently sequential: they pick one token, feed it back in, pick the next token, and so on. You then loop back and let the draft model propose the next batch from the updated context.

The draft model is merely a proposal mechanism—it suggests candidates, but nothing is final until the target model verifies them against its own probability distribution. Any token that survives verification is one the target model would have selected (or at least one that is consistent with its output). The draft model never gets the final say. It just helps you skip ahead through tokens the target model would have produced anyway, rather than waiting for the target to produce them one by one.

So you get a real speedup, sometimes two to three times faster, while the distribution of generated text is bit-for-bit the same as running the big model alone. A hash map starts life as a fixed array of slots, each slot holding either nothing or a reference to a collection of entries. When you ask the map to store a key-value pair, it runs the key through a hash function, which spits out an integer. That integer gets mapped down into the array via a modulo operation, landing on a specific slot. Most of the time, that slot is empty, and you just drop your entry in. But if another key happened to hash to the same slot, you've got a collision.

The most common way to deal with a collision is chaining. Instead of replacing the occupant or erroring out, the slot holds a small list (or sometimes a tree) of entries that all hashed to that slot. When you later look up a key, you hash it, walk to the right slot, and then scan through that small list comparing keys until you find the one you want. In practice, the lists stay very short—usually one or two items—because a good hash function spreads things out. Some implementations switch to open addressing instead, where the map stores entries directly in the array and, on a collision, probes into the *next* slot, then the next, and so on (linear probing, quadratic probing, or a more sophisticated second hash) until it finds an empty slot or an empty marker. Either approach works, but chaining is the one you're most likely to encounter in mainstream languages like Python, Java, and C++.

Now imagine you keep adding entries. The lists at each slot grow longer, and lookups, which should be O(1) on average, start looking more and more like O(n) as you scan through longer chains. To keep things fast, the map tracks its load factor: the ratio of occupied entries to total slots. Once that ratio crosses a threshold—typically around 0.75 to 1.0, depending on the implementation—the map decides the table is getting too crowded.

At that point it resizes. It allocates a new, larger array, usually twice the previous size, and rehashes every single entry that currently lives in the old table. Each key gets its hash recomputed (or rather, its old hash is remapped) into the new, bigger array, and the entries are scattered across the new slots. Because the array is now roughly double the size, the average number of entries landing in any one slot drops back down, and those short chains shrink. The old array gets garbage-collected.

The resizing step is expensive—it touches every entry in the map—so in a single operation it's O(n) rather than O(1). But because it happens so infrequently relative to the many cheap insertions and lookups that precede it, the *amortized* cost of an insert is still O(1) on average. You can think of it like paying for a new, bigger parking lot in one painful afternoon, then spending the next several months driving in and out without ever having to move again. The one-off cost is smoothed out over all the operations that followed.

A hash map starts with an array of slots, often called buckets. When you insert a key, the hash function takes that key and boils it down to an integer, which you then use to pick a slot in the array. Ideally, each key maps to a unique slot, and lookups are fast. In practice, though, two different keys will sometimes hash to the same slot, and that's a collision.

The most common way to deal with a collision is chaining. Each slot doesn't just hold one item; it holds a small list (or linked list) of all the items whose hash pointed there. When you look up a key, you go to the slot and walk through the list, comparing the stored key to the one you're searching for. If the bucket gets too long, lookups slow down from constant time toward linear time, so the list stays short by design. An alternative approach is open addressing. Instead of a list, the map probes the array directly for the next available slot. If slot 42 is taken, it tries 43, then 44, or maybe 42, 44, 46, depending on the probing strategy. The slot you ultimately write into is just the first open one in that probe sequence.

Either way, as you keep inserting items, the array fills up. With chaining, the lists get longer and lookups get slower. With open addressing, you start circling around the array and spending more time on each probe. To keep performance healthy, the hash map watches its load factor, which is the fraction of occupied slots to total slots. Once that ratio crosses a threshold—commonly around 0.7 for open addressing, or a similar number for chaining—the map decides to resize.

Resizing means allocating a larger array, typically double the old size, and then rehashing every existing key into the new, bigger array. This spreads the items out more, shortens the chains or reduces the number of probes needed, and resets the load factor back down to a comfortable level. The cost is that resizing takes time proportional to the number of elements already stored, so it's an occasional expensive step. But because it happens infrequently—each element gets rehashed only every so many insertions—the average cost of an insert or lookup over the lifetime of the map stays constant. That amortized constant-time behavior is the whole point: collisions are inevitable, but the structure keeps them brief by growing before they pile up.

A hash map stores key-value pairs by first running the key through a hash function, which spits out a number. That number points to a slot in an array of buckets. The problem, of course, is that two different keys can hash to the same number. You can't have both keys living in the same slot, so the map needs a plan for the crowded case.

The two most common plans are chaining and open addressing. With chaining, each bucket isn't a single slot but a small linked list. When two keys collide, the second one just gets appended to the list sitting in that bucket. Looking up a key means hashing it, jumping to the right bucket, and walking down the list comparing keys until you find the match. It's simple and forgiving — a bucket can hold many entries — but if your hash function is poor or your data is adversarial, one bucket could balloon into a long chain, and lookups degrade from the hoped-for constant time toward something closer to linear.

Open addressing takes a different approach. There is exactly one slot per bucket, and no separate list. When a key hashes to a slot that's already taken, the map doesn't give up; it probes to the next slot, then the next, and so on, following a deterministic pattern. The simplest pattern is linear probing: check slot *i*, then *i+1*, then *i+2*, and so on, wrapping around the array. Slightly smarter variants use quadratic spacing (skip by 1, then 2, then 3, then 4, in terms of slot offsets) or hash twice and use the second hash to decide the step size, which spreads out the probes more evenly. The downside of any probing scheme is clustering: a run of consecutive filled slots can make subsequent probes march a long way before finding an empty slot, slowing things down.

Either way, the map is watching a ratio called the load factor: the number of keys stored divided by the total number of buckets. When that ratio crosses a threshold — often around three-quarters for chaining, a bit higher for open addressing because probing gets painful when the table is nearly full — the map decides the table is getting too crowded. It allocates a brand-new, larger array, typically twice the old size, and then rehashes every single key it currently holds, inserting each one into the new table. This is the resize. It's expensive in the moment — you're redoing every hash computation and every insertion — but it spreads the keys out so that the next batch of lookups and insertions run fast again. The map doesn't shrink; it just keeps doubling when it hits the ceiling, so the cost of a resize is amortized over the many cheap operations it enables.

So the whole dance is: hash a key, find its slot, deal with any collision through a small list or a probe sequence, keep an eye on how full the table is, and when it gets too packed, build a bigger table and rehash everything from scratch. Most of the time the operations are quick; the occasional resize is the price you pay to keep the average performance where it should be.
